While building codes do not require wind tunnel testing for new skyscrapers, engineers and architects conduct the testing anyway to ensure precision and efficiency during construction. Published July 1, 2006 By Deborah Snoonian Before glass, steel, and concrete, there were plastic, plywood, and pressure sensors. And even in this age of computer-aided design and analysis, engineers still build scale models of buildings to see if the full-sized real ones can withstand strong winds. That explains why in 2002, researchers at the Alan G. Davenport Wind Engineering Group at the University of Western Ontario (UWO) built a 1-to-500 scale replica of 7 World Trade Center and the surrounding neighborhood, measuring about a foot and a half tall. They placed the model carefully inside a boundary-layer wind tunnel, a 128-foot long, 11-foot wide, and 8-foot high apparatus equipped with a wind machine that can simulate everything from gentle breezes to gusts of hurricane intensity. passages.title: How Tall Towers Are Engineered to Withstand Strong Winds
passages.text: Wind creates pressure, turbulence and fluctuating loads. These forces can cause lateral movement and vibration. Engineers respond through several complementary strategies. Aerodynamic shaping can reduce undesirable wind effects. Structural systems provide strength and stiffness. Foundations transfer loads safely into the ground. Wind tunnel testing helps predict how a proposed building will behave. Tuned mass dampers can reduce selected vibrations and improve occupant comfort. Burj Khalifa demonstrates the importance of changing tower geometry and structural organisation. Taipei 101 illustrates how a large tuned mass damper can contribute to motion control. Neither building depends on a single engineering feature. Each relies on an integrated design. The central finding is that tall towers resist wind through the combined use of aerodynamic geometry, strong lateral-load-resisting structures, carefully engineered foundations and, where necessary, vibration-control systems. Modern skyscrapers are therefore not designed simply to withstand wind through brute strength. Their stability comes from understanding how wind behaves and shaping the entire building to respond safely. The Engineering Behind Wind-Resistant Skyscrapers Tall towers are engineered to resist strong winds through a combination of aerodynamic design, structural strength and systems that control movement. Engineers study how wind pressure and turbulence affect buildings, then use reinforced cores, carefully arranged structural members and sometimes specialised dampers to limit sway. Landmark skyscrapers such as Burj Khalifa and Taipei 101 demonstrate how different engineering solutions can make exceptionally tall structures stable and comfortable for occupants. Just what makes these structures so durable? What forces of physics are at play here? Read on to discover innovative ways and methods civil engineers and architects managed to make these towering structures withstand extreme weather and geological events such as high winds or earthquakes. The history of skyscrapers Due to the large number of people who moved from smaller towns to urban areas across the world, big cities sometimes struggled to accommodate this drastic increase in population. Strong winds can lead to various issues such as uncomfortable swaying and shattered windows, and the higher the building’s height-to-width ratio, the more vulnerable it becomes to potentially dangerous geological events. Ultimately, several strategies can be employed to address these challenges. Spiralling structures Spiralling structures, often referred to as “tapered” or “twisted” skyscrapers, are designed with a helical or spiral shape in order to enhance the stability and structural performance of tall buildings. By twisting the building’s form, one can help reduce wind-induced forces as the shape eliminates any continuous vertical edge, ensuring that the wind wraps around the structure instead of hitting a flat plane, consequently reducing its intensity. This aerodynamic advantage enhances the building’s stability in high-wind areas. Another benefit of spiralling structures is the reduction of vortex shedding. Vortex shedding is a phenomenon that occurs when the wind flows around the corner of a building, leading to the formation of alternating low-pressure zones that can cause the structure to sway. How Do Tuned Mass Dampers Reduce Skyscraper Movement? <escape></escape> Some tall buildings use tuned mass dampers to control vibration. A tuned mass damper is a device containing a substantial moving mass connected to the structure through a system that provides stiffness and damping. It is designed to respond to particular frequencies of building motion. When the tower moves, the damper mass moves relative to the structure. This relative motion can reduce the amplitude of the building's vibration. Energy is dissipated through the damping mechanism. The system is not intended to hold the building completely still. Instead, it reduces selected dynamic responses. Tuned mass dampers are especially useful when occupant comfort is a significant concern. Their effectiveness depends on proper tuning and engineering design. The damper must be matched to the relevant dynamic characteristics of the building. Dampers Dampers are crucial structural elements used to stabilise skyscrapers and mitigate the effects of external forces. They help control vibrations and sway, ensuring the safety and comfort of occupants. A main type of damper are tuned mass dampers (TMD), which are large counterweights shaped like a heavy ball that are suspended within the building. They are designed to oscillate in the opposite direction to the building’s natural sway induced by external forces like wind or earthquakes. TMDs are tuned to the building’s specific natural frequency to maximise their effectiveness. Another form of dampers are called viscous dampers. These use the principle of viscous resistance to absorb energy from building motion. They are filled with a viscous fluid, and as the building sways, the fluid’s resistance damps the motion. The goal is to provide sufficient strength, stiffness and stability without using unnecessary material. 5. Why Are Tall Buildings Allowed to Sway? A skyscraper does not need to remain perfectly motionless. In fact, complete rigidity is neither practical nor generally desirable. Structural materials deform slightly when forces act on them. This deformation allows the structure to respond to loading. Engineers calculate how much a building is expected to move under different wind conditions. They examine lateral displacement, acceleration and vibration. Structural safety is one requirement. Occupant comfort is another. A building may remain structurally safe while moving enough to make occupants uncomfortable. People can sometimes perceive slow movement or acceleration even when the displacement is relatively small. This is particularly important near the upper floors of very tall buildings. Engineers therefore establish performance criteria for both structural response and human comfort. The acceptable values depend on building use, applicable standards and design objectives. The challenge is to create a structure that is strong enough to resist extreme loading while limiting everyday movement to suitable levels. 6. How Do Tuned

A tower must be designed to remain safe under the wind conditions specified by applicable structural standards. 2. How Does the Shape of a Tower Reduce Wind Forces? The external shape of a building strongly influences how air moves around it. A simple rectangular tower can produce characteristic patterns of flow separation and vortex shedding. Under certain conditions, these patterns may generate fluctuating forces. Architects and engineers can modify a tower's geometry to reduce undesirable wind effects. Common design approaches include rounded corners, tapered forms, setbacks and changes in building orientation. Some towers have varying cross-sectional shapes at different heights. The system includes a steel spherical mass weighing approximately 660 metric tonnes. The sphere is suspended within the building and connected to damping equipment. When the tower moves under certain dynamic conditions, the mass can move relative to the structure. This movement helps reduce vibration. The damper is unusual because it is visible to visitors. Lateral loads include wind and, where relevant, earthquake forces. Several structural systems are commonly used in tall buildings. Reinforced-Concrete Cores A reinforced-concrete core can provide significant lateral stiffness. It may contain elevators, stairwells and service spaces. The core helps resist bending and twisting caused by wind. Braced Frames Braced frames use diagonal structural members to resist lateral forces. These members can transfer loads through tension and compression. Outrigger Systems Outriggers connect a central core to perimeter columns. This arrangement allows exterior columns to contribute more effectively to resisting overturning. Tube Systems Some tall buildings use closely spaced perimeter columns and beams to create a structural system that behaves partly like a hollow tube. This can provide efficient resistance to lateral loading. Buttressed-Core Systems A buttressed-core system uses structural wings or walls that support one another around a central core. Burj Khalifa is a prominent example. These systems are selected according to building height, geometry, materials and project requirements.
